arms.name: AI-assisted

sources.locator: PDF p. 8, Section 4.2, AI-usage main effect
sources.quote: Regarding novelty, a significant main effect of AI usage was found (Wilks’ λ = 0.872, F(1, 49) = 7.19, p = .010, η²ₚ = 0.13), representing a moderate-to-large effect size.

estimates.notes: Paired crossover comparison: each person contributed an assisted and an unaided task. The table’s combined N counts person-condition observations; n_total counts people once. The reported z is the standardized Wilcoxon signed-rank statistic, and r is retained with its printed nonnegative sign. The paper does not state its formula. Paired-difference SDs and within-person correlations are not reported. A second analysis of this same outcome and sample reports the AI-usage main effect: Wilks’ λ = 0.872, F(1, 49) = 7.19, p = .010, partial η² = 0.13. This additional test is kept here rather than counted as an independent estimate; it is not a test of prior-AI exposure alone.

estimates.notes: Descriptive comparison mapped at screening, not a directly tested contrast in the article. The treatment is prior AI exposure followed by unaided work; the control is unaided work without prior exposure. ai_vs_bau describes this exposure comparison; the screening form used other because the tasks and periods differ. University-spaces output after AI is compared with earlier public-transport output. Task and period are therefore confounded with prior exposure; these arm levels do not isolate an after-AI effect. No p-value, contrast SE, difference, or interval is reported, and no ANOVA interaction or second-period test is attached to this pair. The participant SDs are printed, but no paired comparison applies to these different people. Both outputs were produced in the same session; delay_days is null because no delay in days is printed.

estimates.outcome: Individual-level semantic divergence
estimates.question: with_ai
estimates.measure_detail: Methods describe average pairwise semantic divergence within each participant’s own ideas, but Results describe divergence from a centroid per participant. Descriptions were transcribed with Gemini OCR, manually verified, and embedded with LaBSE (Language-agnostic BERT Sentence Embedding); PDF p. 7, Section 3.3.2.

sources.locator: PDF p. 10, Section 4.3, individual-level semantic divergence
sources.quote: At individual level, the average semantic divergence from the centroid per participant was M= 0.28 (SD = 0.03) for unaided ideas and M= 0.29 (SD = 0.03) for AI-assisted ideas.

sources.locator: PDF p. 10, Section 4.3, individual-level semantic test
sources.quote: A paired samples t-test showed a statistically significant difference, t(364) = 3.41, p = .001, d= 0.48, 95 % CI [0.01, 0.03].

estimates.notes: The printed means place AI-assisted divergence above unaided divergence, while the narrative claims greater semantic concentration with AI (PDF p. 10, Section 4.3; PDF p. 13, Section 5.3). Values and signs are transcribed without correction. The CI is reported beside d without explicitly identifying whether it belongs to the raw difference or effect size; ci_of and paper_effect CI fields are null rather than assuming its target. The standardizer for d is not stated. Analysis-specific participant counts are not printed and cannot be inferred from degrees of freedom, so those counts are null. The methods and results disagree about the distance definition. The reported paired-test degrees of freedom are inconsistent with the stated participant sample; the actual uncertainty unit is unresolved, so se_basis is not_reported. unit and sd_level follow the paper’s per-participant description provisionally, not a verified independence structure.

sources.quote: An independent samples t-test revealed a statistically significant difference between the two conditions, t (728) = −3.54, p < .001, d = −0.26, 95 % CI [−0.03, −0.01].

estimates.notes: The printed means place AI-assisted divergence above unaided divergence, while the narrative claims greater semantic concentration with AI (PDF p. 10, Section 4.3; PDF p. 13, Section 5.3). open_items: Semantic-divergence direction: printed means favor greater divergence with AI, but narrative claims the opposite; labels or interpretation require correction (PDF pp. 10 and 13).

Individual semantic-divergence definition differs between pairwise within-person distances in Methods and centroid distances in Results. The reported t-test df=364 does not establish a participant analysis count; the actual observations and treatment of dependence are unresolved (PDF pp. 7 and 10).

Group semantic-divergence t-test df=728 is printed for a corpus of 728 ideas, with no stated participant adjustment. Verify the actual analysis sample and inferential specification; participant counts are left null for semantic analyses (PDF pp. 5, 7 and 10).
The semantic-divergence confidence intervals have no explicitly named target or subtraction order. Their bounds are retained with ci_of=null; the d standardizers are also unstated (PDF p. 10).
Paired-difference SDs, within-person correlations, and the formula for r are not printed. Do not treat the paired arm counts as independent participants (PDF pp. 6 and 8).
Image-elaboration scorer and word-counting procedure are unidentified, and the exact per-person aggregation of elaboration scores is unstated; measure remains null for both (PDF pp. 6-7, Table 2).
The level of categories used in the category-size test is unspecified (PDF pp. 7 and 10).

Screened after-AI comparisons are descriptive cross-task/cross-period cells with no direct tests. The comparison_type is mapped to prior-AI versus no-prior-AI assistance, but these cells do not isolate the causal effect of previous AI exposure (PDF pp. 5 and 9).
The paper names ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) but supplies no release year or data-collection year; ai_tool.year remains null (PDF p. 5).

Possible participant overlap with c201, DOI 10.1002/cae.22817, remains unconfirmed. The related paper is cited as previous work without a shared-sample statement (PDF pp. 13 and 15; reconciled sample_overlap).

No uncertainty is printed for whole-pool diversity indices and category counts (PDF pp. 9-10). The uniqueness chi-square analyses report arm event counts, retained in notes because the schema has no event-count fields; they are not converted into means or proportions.
The article offers data on request but supplies no public data or code link, supplement, or appendix in the document (PDF p. 15, Data availability).
